paragraphs: Zanaflex is indicated for spasticity in adults. Its brief therapeutic effect favors selected activities/times when relief is most needed. Supporting trials included multiple sclerosis and spinal cord injury; reduced muscle tone did not consistently translate to improved daily-function measures. Do not imply approval for every acute musculoskeletal pain syndrome.

Assess goals, useful residual tone, mobility, fall risk and sedative/antihypertensive therapy before treatment. Some patients rely on tone for standing or balance, so reduction can impair function. This focused profile covers selected oral tablets/capsules for adult spasticity; pediatric and off-label acute-pain protocols are outside scope. Tizanidine is not a controlled substance, but dependence/rebound can occur.

Start 2 mg by mouth every 6–8 hours as needed, at most three doses in 24 hours. Increase each dose by 2–4 mg at intervals of 1–4 days according to response/tolerability. Maximum total 36 mg/day; single doses >16 mg have not been studied. Do not mistake that study ceiling for a routine target—higher single doses produce more hypotension/sedation. Use only the prescribed activity-related doses.

May be taken with or without food, but consistently use the same relationship to meals and the prescribed form. Tablets/capsules are bioequivalent fasting, not fed. Food raises tablet exposure differently from capsules. Sprinkling capsule contents on applesauce also changes exposure versus the intact fasting capsule; do not open or switch without explicit prescribing/pharmacy instructions. Monitor response and adverse effects after any food/form change.

CrCl <25 mL/min or hepatic impairment: use lower individual doses while titrating. If higher doses are required, increase individual doses rather than frequency, guided by tolerability; no fixed percentage reduction is specified. Monitor closely for excessive sedation, dizziness, dry mouth, weakness and hypotension. Obtain aminotransferases at baseline and one month after the maximum dose is reached, or when injury is suspected.

The label recommends lowering total daily dosage by 2–4 mg per day when discontinuing, especially after high doses/prolonged use or with opioids, to limit rebound. Individualize with the clinician; do not suddenly stop regular therapy. This often-as-needed medicine should not be doubled to replace an omitted dose or compressed into shorter intervals; follow the prescribed schedule and discuss interruptions of chronic use.

items: Hypotension, orthostatic effects, bradycardia and syncope can occur. Review blood pressure and symptoms before increasing; monitor with antihypertensives and rise carefully. Another alpha₂ agonist is not recommended.

Hepatocellular injury can occur. Check aminotransferases before treatment, one month after maximum dose and whenever injury is suspected; promptly assess jaundice/dark urine or other compatible symptoms.
Sedation can impair driving/activity and add to alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants. Monitor falls, alertness and breathing when combinations are necessary.
Hallucinations/delusions or psychotic symptoms warrant reassessment and consideration of discontinuation.
Anaphylaxis or throat/tongue swelling requires stopping and immediate care.
Abrupt withdrawal can cause rebound hypertension, tachycardia and hypertonia, particularly after high/prolonged dosing or with narcotics. Use the clinician-directed reduction plan.
Reduced spasticity can compromise posture/balance in a patient who depends on tone; assess functional outcome, not only muscle-tone reduction.

paragraphs: Strong CYP1A2 inhibitors, including fluvoxamine and ciprofloxacin, are contraindicated. A history of hypersensitivity to tizanidine or the exact product’s ingredients is also contraindicated; anaphylaxis/angioedema have occurred. Other CYP1A2 inhibitors have avoidance/review recommendations, not the same blanket formal contraindication status.

No boxed warning appears in the selected current Zanaflex label. Significant interaction-related hypotension/sedation, liver injury, severe allergy and withdrawal warnings still require careful prescribing.

Common reported effects are dry mouth, somnolence/sedation, weakness/fatigue and dizziness; constipation, nausea/vomiting, liver-test changes and hypotension/bradycardia also occur. Serious postmarketing hepatic, allergic, skin, cardiac and neuropsychiatric reports cannot define incidence. Overdose can cause coma, respiratory depression, marked hypotension and bradycardia and may be fatal: emergency airway/cardiorespiratory support and Poison Help guidance (U.S. 1-800-222-1222). Dialysis is unlikely to remove tizanidine efficiently.

rows: Contraindicated; greatly increased exposure can cause severe hypotension, drowsiness and impaired function.

Avoid if possible: label examples include zileuton, selected antiarrhythmics (amiodarone, mexiletine, propafenone, verapamil), cimetidine/famotidine, acyclovir and ticlopidine. If necessary and hypotension/bradycardia/excess sedation develops, reduce or discontinue.
Combination not recommended; may reduce clearance. If necessary, monitor and reduce/discontinue for hypotension, bradycardia or drowsiness.
Alcohol / opioids / benzodiazepines / tricyclics / other CNS depressants
Alcohol raises exposure and CNS effects are additive. Avoid alcohol; closely review necessary sedative combinations.
Not recommended due to cumulative hypotension.
Additive hypotension; monitor blood pressure and symptoms.

paragraphs: Human pregnancy data are inadequate; animal studies show developmental mortality/growth effects, so discuss maternal need and alternatives before or during pregnancy. Human milk/infant/milk-production data are absent, although animal milk transfer occurs; balance breastfeeding benefit with maternal need and possible infant risk. Human fertility data are inadequate; animal fertility effects do not establish a quantified human risk.

Pediatric safety/effectiveness is not established; no pediatric dose is supplied here. Older-adult trials were limited, and PK comparisons found slower clearance in older subjects. Review kidney function, start cautiously and monitor sedation, hypotension, falls and function; older adults with CrCl <25 need lower individual titration doses.

Clearance is reduced in severe renal insufficiency; in studied older patients with CrCl <25 it was more than 50% lower than healthy older subjects. Use lower doses and monitor rather than inferring an exact percentage dose conversion. Hepatic PK has not been evaluated, but extensive hepatic metabolism predicts important exposure changes; caution, lower doses and liver testing are recommended.

A central alpha₂ agonist thought to increase presynaptic inhibition of motor neurons, with effects greatest on polysynaptic pathways and reduced facilitation of spinal motor neurons. The same class activity contributes to hypotension and sedation.

facts: Essentially fully absorbed, but oral bioavailability ~40% from extensive first-pass metabolism. Fasting peak ~1 hour; food/form changes alter this.
Parent half-life ~2–2.5 hours in studied conditions; ~95% metabolized, mainly by CYP1A2. Metabolites are not known to be active.
Radiolabeled recovery ~60% in urine and ~20% in feces; this includes metabolites and is not 60% unchanged renal clearance.
Peak tone reduction ~1–2 hours and effect wanes over several hours in trials; do not use PK averages to shorten the labeled 6–8-hour interval.

paragraphs: Follow spasticity relief, mobility/posture/balance, alertness, dizziness, blood pressure/pulse and falls, especially during titration or medicine changes. Review renal function in at-risk/older patients. Check aminotransferases at baseline, one month after maximum dose and if liver injury is suspected. Ask about hallucinations, sedatives, food/form consistency and withdrawal symptoms.

Take only the prescribed form/dose with a consistent meal pattern; tell every prescriber/pharmacist before starting or stopping a medicine. Avoid alcohol and hazardous activity until effects are known; rise slowly. Do not abruptly discontinue chronic use. Airway swelling, inability to wake, severe fainting or breathing impairment needs emergency care. Seek prompt review for jaundice, hallucinations or severe rebound symptoms.

Zanaflex 4 mg scored tablet is the representative product. Its current label covers tablets and 2/4/6 mg capsules; an Apotex tablet label separately verifies 2 mg and 4 mg generic tablets. Exact appearance/ingredients differ by manufacturer; use dispensing records rather than appearance alone.

rows: 4 mg quadrisected tablet (A594); capsules 2, 4 and 6 mg.
2 mg bisected tablet (APO / TI-2); 4 mg quadrisected tablet (APO / TI-4).
Label mg expresses tizanidine base supplied as hydrochloride. Confirm the prescribed base-equivalent mg and product.

paragraphs: Zanaflex: 20–25°C, excursions 15–30°C, child-resistant container. Selected Apotex tablets: same temperature range, tight light-resistant container. Keep securely away from children and follow the dispensed product’s instructions; do not apply capsule/food-handling assumptions to every generic product.

validationEvidence.caveat: Local checks and representative visual inspection passed; production deployment pending.

sources.title: Farxiga · Current full prescribing information
sources.note: Clinical revision June 2026; SPL49 effective June 3, 2026. Product-specific renal/indication limits and updated genitourinary warning.

assertions: Farxiga reduces sustained eGFR decline, end-stage kidney disease, cardiovascular death and heart-failure hospitalization in adults with CKD at risk of progression. In adults with heart failure, it reduces cardiovascular death, heart-failure hospitalization and urgent heart-failure visits. The HF indication is not restricted to reduced ejection fraction in the current label.

With diet/exercise, it improves glycemic control in adults and children age 10 years or older with type 2 diabetes. It also reduces heart-failure hospitalization in adults with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease or multiple cardiovascular risk factors. That latter adult indication is not equivalent to an unrestricted claim of prevention of all cardiovascular events.

It is not recommended to improve glucose control in type 1 diabetes or in type 2 diabetes when eGFR <45 mL/min/1.73 m². For CKD it is not recommended with polycystic kidney disease or kidney disease requiring/recently treated with immunosuppression. This monotherapy profile does not supply fixed-combination dapagliflozin/metformin or saxagliptin regimens.

Start 5 mg orally once daily; increase to 10 mg once daily if additional glucose control is needed. This adult/pediatric type 2 diabetes regimen applies at eGFR ≥45 mL/min/1.73 m². Below 45, glucose-lowering use is not recommended because it is likely ineffective; do not infer a cardiorenal pediatric indication.

sourceAudit.card: Adult cardiorenal dosing and renal strata
assertions: For the adult CKD, HF and type 2 diabetes/HF-hospitalization indications, the dose is 10 mg once daily. The table separates initiation from continuation; all eGFR values are mL/min/1.73 m².

rows: 10 mg once daily for eligible adult non-glycemic indications
May continue 10 mg once daily for labeled kidney/CV/HF risk reduction

assertions: Check renal function and volume status before starting; correct volume depletion first. Take orally once daily with or without food. If a dose is missed, take it as soon as possible and do not double the next dose.

Withhold at least 3 days, if possible, before surgery or a procedure involving prolonged fasting. Temporary clinical states predisposing to ketoacidosis may also require withholding under the care plan. Resume when clinically stable and eating again; after ketoacidosis, monitor for resolution before restart. Do not stop or markedly reduce prescribed insulin on your own.

No dose change is recommended solely for older age or mild/moderate/severe hepatic impairment. Severe hepatic impairment nevertheless needs an individualized benefit-risk assessment because specific efficacy/safety studies are lacking. This is not a claim of equal risk in all liver conditions.

Suspect ketoacidosis with nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, malaise or shortness of breath even if glucose is normal or <250 mg/dL. Risk rises with missed/reduced insulin, acute illness, fasting/poor intake, ketogenic diet, surgery, dehydration, alcohol misuse or pancreatic disease. Stop the drug and obtain urgent evaluation for suspected ketoacidosis; glucosuria/ketosis may persist beyond discontinuation.

Assess hydration, pressure and renal function. Volume depletion/hypotension and acute kidney injury are more likely with impaired renal function, older age or loop diuretics. Correct volume depletion before starting. Insulin/secretagogue combinations can increase hypoglycemia; any reduction must be individualized without precipitating under-insulinization.

Monitor/treat genital and urinary infections promptly. Urosepsis, pyelonephritis and Fournier’s gangrene can require hospitalization; perineal/genital pain, redness or swelling with fever/malaise needs immediate assessment and discontinuation if necrotizing infection is suspected. Serious allergy requires stopping and urgent care.

A history of serious hypersensitivity to dapagliflozin or any Farxiga excipient is contraindicated. The current label does not list a separate dialysis contraindication; initiation evidence/renal limits must still be respected rather than treating absence of a contraindication as approval to start on dialysis.
The reviewed current Farxiga label contains no FDA boxed warning. Its potentially fatal ketoacidosis and serious infection warnings still apply to all eligible indications.

Commonly reported effects include genital mycotic infections, urinary tract infections, increased urination and nasopharyngitis. Volume depletion, ketoacidosis, severe GU infection, hypersensitivity and acute kidney injury are important serious events. Small early creatinine rises/eGFR falls may stabilize within about 2 weeks; changes outside that pattern merit evaluation rather than automatic attribution to an expected effect.

Insulin or sulfonylurea doses may need clinician-directed reduction to limit hypoglycemia. Do not make an indiscriminate insulin reduction: under-insulinization is a ketoacidosis trigger. Increase glucose surveillance with treatment changes.

SGLT2 inhibitors may lower serum lithium concentrations; monitor lithium more often during initiation and dose changes. Loop diuretics increase susceptibility to volume depletion/hypotension; reassess volume, pressure and renal function rather than inferring a universal diuretic reduction.

Glucosuria is expected from the mechanism and can produce a positive urine glucose test; use other measures for glucose control. The 1,5-anhydroglucitol assay is also unreliable during SGLT2 therapy. These findings do not exclude ketoacidosis, which needs its own assessment.

Glycemic-control safety/effectiveness are established from age 10; under 10 is not established. Pediatric CKD/HF/cardiovascular risk-reduction indications are not established. Older adults need no age-only dose change but are more susceptible to hypotension and require volume/renal surveillance.

Use the indication-specific 45 and 25 thresholds. Trials did not enroll people with eGFR <25 or already on dialysis; some enrolled patients continued after eGFR decline or dialysis initiation. That continuation evidence does not create a universal recommendation to initiate dialysis treatment. Reassess response, volume and kidney function individually.

Not recommended in the second/third trimesters because animal findings raise developing-kidney concerns; limited human pregnancy data cannot establish safety. Not recommended while breastfeeding because infant renal-development risk is possible. Severe hepatic impairment requires individualized benefit-risk assessment despite no specified dose adjustment.

Dapagliflozin increases urinary glucose excretion and sodium delivery distally, with associated effects on volume and intraglomerular pressure. Glucosuria typically approaches baseline about 3 days after stopping, but longer persistence is reported; half-life alone should not determine perioperative safety.

Fasting peak concentration is usually reached within about 2 hours and oral bioavailability is about 78% at 10 mg. It is about 91% protein-bound, metabolized mainly by UGT1A9 to an inactive glucuronide and eliminated predominantly as metabolites via urine. Mean terminal half-life is about 12.9 hours. Food does not meaningfully alter total exposure.

Renal impairment raises systemic exposure but reduces urinary glucose excretion, explaining the glycemic limitation. Approved adult HF/CKD outcomes and their dosing are based on separate trials and thresholds. Do not infer greater glucose lowering from a higher plasma concentration.

Assess renal function before initiation and as clinically indicated; evaluate volume and pressure, particularly with diuretics, older age or impaired kidney function. Track glucose for diabetes goals and adult HF/CKD outcomes through the clinical plan. Consider ketone monitoring when risk or symptoms warrant; do not use urine glucose or 1,5-AG to judge glycemic control.

Explain the 3-day preoperative hold and clinically stable/oral-intake restart criteria. Avoid unplanned insulin reduction and discuss poor intake, dehydration, illness, ketogenic diets and alcohol use. Get immediate help for ketosis symptoms or painful swollen/red perineal tissue with fever/malaise; report urinary/genital infection symptoms promptly. Fluid intake should follow the individualized HF/CKD plan.

Seek poison-service or medical advice after excess ingestion; treatment is supportive according to clinical status. Removal by hemodialysis has not been studied, so do not claim dialysis is an established antidote.

AstraZeneca Farxiga 10 mg is yellow, biconvex and diamond-shaped with 10 and 1428 on opposite sides; 30-count NDC 0310-6210-30. The 5 mg tablet is yellow and round with 5 and 1427; 30-count NDC 0310-6205-30. Verify the actual product label.

Reviewed film-coated tablets supply 5 or 10 mg dapagliflozin. These strengths are not interchangeable with fixed combinations based on their total tablet weight; no injectable or pediatric liquid regimen is supplied.
Store at 20–25°C, with permitted excursions of 15–30°C. Dispense with the Medication Guide and keep safely away from children.

sources.title: Percocet tablets · Current full prescribing information
sources.note: Clinical revision August 2026; current SPL65 effective September 23, 2026. Full opioid/APAP combination label, updated lactation and overdose-reversal wording.

assertions: Percocet treats pain severe enough to require an opioid when alternatives are inadequate. Reserve it for alternatives that are ineffective, not tolerated or insufficient. Addiction, overdose and death can occur at any dose or duration; many acute conditions need only a few days when an opioid is necessary.

sources.sections: INDICATIONS AND USAGE; DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION, Important Dosage and Administration Instructions

assertions: This profile covers current immediate-release oral Percocet tablets containing oxycodone hydrochloride plus 325 mg acetaminophen. It does not establish single-ingredient oxycodone, extended-release oxycodone, liquid or another combination product dosing. A fixed combination limits independent titration of the components.

sources.sections: DESCRIPTION; DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION, Initial Dosage; HOW SUPPLIED

assertions: For first opioid use, the label starts with 2.5 mg/325 mg tablets, 1–2 tablets every 6 hours as needed, at the lowest dose achieving adequate analgesia. The usual adult regimen for the other reviewed strengths is one tablet every 6 hours as needed. Individualize for prior exposure, pain and respiratory/addiction risk; do not self-escalate.

sources.sections: DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION, Initial Dosage; Important Dosage and Administration Instructions

assertions: The table reproduces labeled maximal tablet counts and calculated acetaminophen totals, not a recommendation to reach them. Some ceiling counts exceed what the usual six-hour schedule supplies; do not change frequency to reach a ceiling. Follow the lower limit set by the prescription, clinical risks, product ceiling and total daily acetaminophen.

sources.sections: DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION, Initial Dosage; WARNINGS, Hepatotoxicity

assertions: The product label requires total acetaminophen not to exceed 4,000 mg/day from all sources. Do not add another APAP-containing medicine without advice; check OTC cold/pain labels. This ceiling is not a universally safe target, especially with liver disease or alcohol use, and it does not authorize extra opioid tablets. Suspected excess requires immediate medical assessment even if the person feels well.

sources.sections: DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION, Initial Dosage; WARNINGS, Hepatotoxicity; Information for Patients/Caregivers

assertions: Reevaluate pain source, benefit, sedation/respiration and adverse effects before increasing. Worsening pain after an increase may reflect opioid-induced hyperalgesia rather than a need for more opioid. Relative bioavailability versus extended-release oxycodone is unknown in this label; conversion can cause excessive sedation/respiratory depression and needs a specific clinician plan.

sources.sections: DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION, Titration and Maintenance; Conversion; WARNINGS, Opioid-Induced Hyperalgesia

assertions: Start below the usual dose in hepatic or renal impairment and titrate carefully while monitoring sedation, respiration and hypotension. Older adults should generally start low and titrate slowly. The label supplies no fixed eGFR, dialysis or Child-Pugh conversion table; the acetaminophen component also requires liver-risk assessment.

sources.sections: PRECAUTIONS, Geriatric Use; Hepatic Impairment; Renal Impairment; WARNINGS, Hepatotoxicity

assertions: Do not abruptly stop or rapidly taper a physically dependent patient. Agree on an individualized taper and follow-up plan; the label illustrates reductions no greater than 10–25% of the total daily opioid dose every 2–4 weeks, with adjustments for duration, withdrawal, pain and mental health. This is not a compulsory universal schedule. A missed dose is followed by the next usual prescribed dose, not a double dose.

sources.sections: DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION, Safe Reduction or Discontinuation; Medication Guide

assertions: Respiratory depression can occur even at recommended doses, especially at initiation/increase, with lung disease, older/debilitated status or CNS depressants. Accidental ingestion of even one dose by a child can be fatal. Assess addiction/misuse risk and reassess throughout therapy; sleep-related breathing disorders may require a dose review.

Monitor severe hypotension, adrenal-insufficiency symptoms, seizures, biliary/pancreatic symptoms and constipation. Avoid circulatory shock and impaired consciousness/coma. Head injury/increased intracranial pressure require extra sedation/respiration surveillance. Dysphagia/regurgitation or noncardiac chest pain may reflect opioid-induced esophageal dysfunction.

Acetaminophen can cause liver failure and severe skin/allergic reactions. Stop and assess rash or serious hypersensitivity. OIH may cause paradoxical worsening pain; do not independently raise the dose. Rapid withdrawal can cause uncontrolled pain, severe withdrawal and psychological harm.

sources.sections: WARNINGS, Addiction; Respiratory Depression; Hepatotoxicity; OIH; Chronic Pulmonary Disease; Adrenal Insufficiency; Hypotension; Skin Reactions; Intracranial Pressure; GI Conditions; Seizures; Withdrawal

assertions: Significant respiratory depression; acute/severe bronchial asthma in an unmonitored setting or without resuscitative equipment; known/suspected GI obstruction including paralytic ileus; or hypersensitivity to oxycodone, acetaminophen or another ingredient.

sourceAudit.card: Boxed warning: opioid and hepatotoxicity risks
assertions: The current box covers addiction/abuse/misuse, life-threatening respiratory depression, accidental ingestion, benzodiazepine/CNS-depressant combinations, neonatal withdrawal, opioid REMS, CYP3A4 interactions and acetaminophen hepatotoxicity. These risks persist despite correct prescribing; assess, counsel and monitor rather than treating a labeled tablet ceiling as assurance of safety.

Frequently observed effects include dizziness/lightheadedness, sedation, nausea/vomiting, constipation and itching. Serious events include apnea/respiratory arrest, hypotension/shock, liver toxicity, anaphylaxis, serious skin reactions, serotonin syndrome and adrenal insufficiency. Prolonged opioid use may affect androgen levels/fertility. Postmarketing hypoglycemia and OIED are also reported; frequency/causality cannot be inferred from spontaneous reports.

sources.sections: ADVERSE REACTIONS; CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY, Endocrine Effects

assertions: Macrolides, azole antifungals and protease inhibitors can increase oxycodone exposure and fatal respiratory depression risk; combined CYP3A4/CYP2D6 inhibition may amplify effects. Adding an inducer such as rifampin/carbamazepine/phenytoin may reduce effect or provoke withdrawal; stopping an inducer can raise exposure. Starting/stopping either class needs frequent reassessment and clinician-directed dose adjustment.

sources.sections: WARNINGS, CYP3A4 Interaction; PRECAUTIONS, Drug Interactions

sourceAudit.card: CNS depressants, alcohol and muscle relaxants
assertions: Benzodiazepines, sedative-hypnotics, gabapentinoids, antipsychotics, other opioids, muscle relaxants and alcohol can produce profound sedation, hypotension, respiratory depression, coma or death. Reserve unavoidable combinations for inadequate alternatives, use the lowest effective doses/durations and provide rescue/caregiver education. Avoid alcohol, which also increases acetaminophen liver risk.

sources.sections: WARNINGS, CNS Depressants; Hepatotoxicity; Drug Interactions; Medication Guide

assertions: SSRIs/SNRIs, TCAs, tramadol, certain muscle relaxants and other serotonergic agents may cause serotonin syndrome; monitor during initiation/adjustment and stop/evaluate if suspected. Percocet is not recommended with MAOIs or within 14 days after stopping them, including relevant linezolid/methylene-blue exposures. Urgent exceptions require supervised specialist management, not a self-directed regimen.

sources.sections: PRECAUTIONS, Drug Interactions, Serotonergic Drugs; MAOIs

sourceAudit.card: Other opioid, GI and diuretic interactions
assertions: Mixed agonist/antagonist or partial-agonist analgesics may reduce analgesia or precipitate withdrawal; opioid transitions need a clinician plan. Anticholinergics can worsen constipation/urinary retention/ileus; monitor symptoms. Opioids may blunt diuresis and affect pressure; monitor diuretic response. The label also describes acetaminophen interactions including reduced lamotrigine levels; review the complete list when relevant.

Use only after individualized benefit-risk assessment. Extended use in pregnancy can cause life-threatening neonatal opioid withdrawal requiring specialist management. Placental transfer can cause neonatal sedation/respiratory depression; the label does not recommend use during/immediately before labor when other analgesic techniques are more appropriate.

sources.sections: WARNINGS, NOWS; PRECAUTIONS, Pregnancy; Labor or Delivery

assertions: Both components enter milk. The current label reports low relative infant oxycodone exposure in a limited postpartum study but still requires observation for unusual sleepiness, breathing trouble or limpness and immediate care if these occur. Its <60 mg/day research statement is not a universal breastfeeding safety limit or dosing recommendation. Infant withdrawal can occur if maternal opioid therapy or breastfeeding stops.

sources.sections: PRECAUTIONS, Nursing Mothers; Information for Patients/Caregivers

assertions: Pediatric safety/effectiveness are not established. Older, cachectic/debilitated and chronic-lung-disease patients have greater respiratory-depression risk, even at recommended doses; consider alternatives and frequent reassessment when initiating/titrating.

sources.sections: PRECAUTIONS, Pediatric Use; Geriatric Use; WARNINGS, Chronic Pulmonary Disease

assertions: Reduced clearance/prolonged half-life can increase opioid effects. Start lower and monitor sedation, respiration and pressure. Underlying liver disease and alcohol also raise APAP liver-injury risk; evaluate whether a fixed combination is appropriate rather than assuming a normal-dose APAP ceiling applies.

sources.sections: PRECAUTIONS, Hepatic Impairment; Renal Impairment; WARNINGS, Hepatotoxicity

assertions: Oxycodone is a full opioid agonist with relative mu-receptor selectivity; respiratory-center depression and GI motility reduction accompany analgesia. Acetaminophen’s analgesic mechanism is incompletely established and thought to involve central actions. The absence of an oxycodone analgesic ceiling does not mean this fixed combination can be escalated without limit.

sources.sections: CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY, Mechanism; Pharmacodynamics; DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION

assertions: Oral oxycodone is substantially absorbed and metabolized to noroxycodone mainly through CYP3A and oxymorphone through CYP2D6, with subsequent conjugation. Organ impairment and pathway interactions can prolong effects; use actual response and monitoring rather than assuming equal exposure across patients.

sources.sections: CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY, Pharmacokinetics; PRECAUTIONS, Drug Interactions; Hepatic/Renal Impairment

assertions: Acetaminophen is rapidly absorbed, primarily glucuronidated/sulfated in the liver and excreted as metabolites through urine. A minor oxidative pathway creates a reactive metabolite normally detoxified by glutathione; overdose can cause delayed hepatic necrosis. Its labeled plasma half-life is about 1.25–3 hours and may lengthen with liver injury/overdose.

sources.sections: CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY, Metabolism and Elimination; OVERDOSAGE

assertions: Reassess pain source, function, benefit, sedation/respiration, constipation, hypotension, interactions and signs of misuse/addiction. Check liver/renal risks and all APAP sources; worsening pain may require assessment for OIH rather than automatic escalation. Tapering needs ongoing care and mood/withdrawal monitoring.

sources.sections: WARNINGS; PRECAUTIONS, Information for Patients/Caregivers; DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION

assertions: Discuss an accessible opioid-overdose reversal agent, such as naloxone or nalmefene, with patient and caregivers; products differ in route, strength and approved ages. For suspected overdose, call emergency services even after reversal. Reversal may wear off before oxycodone does and repeat dosing/medical observation may be necessary under the rescue product instructions. Reversal does not treat acetaminophen liver injury.

sources.sections: WARNINGS, Patient Access; DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION, Patient Access; OVERDOSAGE

assertions: Get immediate medical/poison-service help even before symptoms. Clinicians assess acetaminophen levels and the exposure history and use N-acetylcysteine promptly when indicated; delayed absorption or combination overdose may complicate interpretation. Do not apply a home treatment rule or wait for jaundice/liver pain.

Do not share, self-increase, mix with alcohol or drive until effects are known. Store securely away from children and visitors; even one accidental dose can be fatal. Prefer prompt take-back disposal; if unavailable, follow the current label/FDA instructions for this flush-listed opioid. Read the Medication Guide and know when constipation or sedation needs care.

sources.sections: PRECAUTIONS, Information for Patients/Caregivers; Medication Guide

assertions: Current Percocet 5 mg/325 mg is a blue round tablet marked PERCOCET and 5 on one side with a bisect on the other; 100-count NDC 63481-623-70. Current label manufacturing is for SpecGx with Par Health copyright; do not assume an older Endo company listing establishes the current package.

sources.sections: HOW SUPPLIED; storage/manufacturer footer, Revised August 2026

assertions: Oral IR tablets: 2.5/325, 5/325, 7.5/325 or 10/325 mg oxycodone hydrochloride/acetaminophen. Product strength is stated as the hydrochloride, not recalculated oxycodone base. All are Schedule II controlled substances. Different generic combinations or liquids require their own labels.

sources.sections: DESCRIPTION; DRUG ABUSE AND DEPENDENCE; HOW SUPPLIED

assertions: Store at 20–25°C, protect from moisture and dispense in a tight light-resistant container. Keep securely out of reach/sight of children and inaccessible to others; arrange prompt safe disposal when no longer needed.

sources.sections: Storage; Information for Patients/Caregivers; Medication Guide
